title: The Passover and the Night Israel Went Free
summary: God gives Moses and Aaron instructions for the first Passover: each household is to kill an unblemished lamb, put its blood on the doorframe, and eat the meat roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, dressed and ready to leave. At midnight the LORD strikes down the firstborn of Egypt and passes over the houses marked with blood. Pharaoh sends Israel out that night, the Egyptians give them silver, gold, and clothing, and after 430 years in Egypt the Israelites march out from Rameses, with rules added for how the Passover is to be kept forever.
story:
Everything in Exodus so far has been leading to this night. At the bush God promised to strike Egypt with wonders and bring his people out (3:20), and before Moses reached Egypt God told him to warn Pharaoh, “Israel is My firstborn son” and “I will kill your firstborn son” if Pharaoh refused to let him go (4:22-23). Nine plagues have been warnings, each refused, and chapter 11 announced the last. Now the tenth plague falls, and it falls differently from the others. In several earlier plagues God set Israel apart without any act on their part (8:22; 9:4, 26); this time protection comes through a lamb, its blood, and a meal eaten in obedience.

The chapter moves back and forth between that first night and every later Passover, because the event and its remembrance belong together. God's instructions for the night (verses 1-13) are followed at once by instructions for the yearly feast (14-20), then Moses passes the command to the elders (21-28), then the night itself happens (29-36), then Israel marches (37-42), and finally a rule settles who may eat (43-51). By the end Israel is out of Egypt, a vast company on the road from Rameses to Succoth, and the book's first great movement, from slavery to release, is complete. The consecration of the firstborn follows in chapter 13, the sea still lies ahead in chapter 14, and Sinai lies beyond it.
historical:
The Passover falls in spring, in the month called Abib (13:4; Deuteronomy 16:1), a word connected with fresh ears of grain. After the Babylonian exile the Jews adopted Babylonian month names, and the same month is called Nisan (Nehemiah 2:1; Esther 3:7). Verse 2 makes it the first month of the year, so that Israel's calendar of worship begins with its redemption, though Israel also knew a year that turned in the autumn; the Mishnah names four new years, with Nisan the new year for kings and festivals (m. Rosh Hashanah 1:1). Since the month began with the new moon, the fourteenth fell at the full moon, so the night of the Passover was a moonlit one. The lamb was to be killed ‘between the two evenings’; the Pharisaic and later rabbinic reading took this as the afternoon, and by the Second Temple period the lambs were slaughtered at the temple in the afternoon of the fourteenth, the priests passing the blood in basins to the altar (m. Pesachim 5:1-6). Josephus says the victims were killed from the ninth to the eleventh hour, roughly three to five in the afternoon, and reports a count of 256,500 lambs at one Passover under the governor Cestius in the 60s AD (Jewish War 6.423-425), a figure most historians think inflated but which shows the scale of the feast.

The Old Testament records several notable Passovers after this one: at Sinai (Numbers 9:1-14), at Gilgal on entering the land (Joshua 5:10-12), under Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 30), under Josiah, who kept a Passover unlike any since the days of the judges (2 Kings 23:21-23; 2 Chronicles 35), and after the return from exile (Ezra 6:19-22). The earliest evidence outside the Bible is the so-called Passover Papyrus from Elephantine, a Jewish military colony on the Nile in southern Egypt. In a letter of about 419 BC, a man named Hananiah writes to Jedaniah and the Jewish garrison that King Darius II has authorized them to keep the festival of unleavened bread from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of Nisan, with instructions not to work on the first and last days and to keep leaven out of their houses.

Verse 37 has Israel leaving from Rameses, the Delta city of the store cities in 1:11, generally identified with Pi-Ramesses, the capital of Ramesses II (about 1279-1213 BC), at Qantir beside the older site of Tell el-Dab'a (ancient Avaris). Succoth is widely identified with Egyptian Tjeku in the Wadi Tumilat, the valley running east from the Delta toward the Bitter Lakes, often at Tell el-Maskhuta, which Édouard Naville excavated in 1883 and took to be Pithom. Those who date the exodus to the fifteenth century BC take the name Rameses as an updating of an older place name, as in Genesis 47:11. No Egyptian text mentions the death of the firstborn or Israel's departure, and historians weigh that silence differently: Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman (The Bible Unearthed, 2001) treat the exodus as a later national epic, while James Hoffmeier (Israel in Egypt, 1997) argues that the Egyptian background of the story is genuine and early, and that Egyptian royal records rarely record defeats.

The number of about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children, would mean a total population of two million or more. Some interpreters take the figure as it stands, noting that it agrees with the census totals of Numbers 1:46 and 26:51. Others argue that the Hebrew word elef, ‘thousand’, can also name a clan or a military unit (Judges 6:15), a line of argument taken up by Flinders Petrie, by George Mendenhall (Journal of Biblical Literature 77, 1958), and by Colin Humphreys (Vetus Testamentum 48, 1998), which would make the company far smaller. The 430 years of verse 40 are also counted in more than one way (see the text note below).
cultural:
The Passover is a household meal. Each father's house takes a lamb or kid, a year-old male without blemish from the sheep or the goats, and a small family shares with its nearest neighbor (verses 3-5); the Hebrew seh covers both sheep and goats, so ‘lamb’ is a narrower English choice than the text requires. The animal was the best of the flock, not a leftover. It was kept four days, killed at twilight, roasted whole over the fire, head, legs, and inner parts together, and eaten entirely that night; anything left was burned. The early rabbinic commentary on Exodus, the Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael (Pisha 5), asked why the lamb was taken four days early and answered that Israel, ‘naked’ of commandments by which to be redeemed (Ezekiel 16:7), was given two to perform: the blood of the Passover and the blood of circumcision.

The bread was unleavened, made without the lump of fermented dough (se'or) kept back from a previous batch to make new dough rise, and the herbs were bitter. The text does not say which herbs; the Mishnah lists lettuce, chicory, and similar plants (m. Pesachim 2:6), and later tradition read them as a taste of the bitterness of slavery, since 1:14 says the Egyptians made Israel's lives bitter with the same Hebrew root. Deuteronomy calls the unleavened loaves “the bread of affliction” eaten “in haste” (Deuteronomy 16:3). The command to remove all leaven from the house (verse 15) is the origin of the Jewish custom of searching the house for leaven by lamplight on the eve of Passover (m. Pesachim 1:1).

The blood was applied with hyssop, a small bushy plant usually identified with Syrian marjoram (Origanum syriacum), whose hairy stems hold liquid and which was used for sprinkling in rites of cleansing (Leviticus 14:4-6; Numbers 19:18); a psalmist prays, “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean” (Psalm 51:7). It went on the doorposts and the lintel, the frame through which anyone entering had to pass. Doorways carried religious weight across the ancient Near East, and Mesopotamian households buried protective figures under thresholds; Exodus uses a gesture its first readers would have recognized and gives it new content, since the blood protects only because God said he would see it. The Hebrew word for doorpost, mezuzah, later gave its name to the small case holding verses of Scripture that Jewish families fix to their doorframes (Deuteronomy 6:9).

The firstborn son held a special place in the ancient household as heir and as the family's continuation, and in Egypt Pharaoh's heir was the next divine king. That is why the last plague strikes at the firstborn, and why Israel's own firstborn are afterward consecrated to God and redeemed (13:1-2, 11-16). The meal is eaten dressed for the road, robe tucked into the belt, sandals on, staff in hand (verse 11), by people who expect to walk out before morning.

After the temple's destruction in AD 70 the lamb could no longer be sacrificed, and the rabbinic Seder, described in the Mishnah (m. Pesachim 10), became the Jewish form of the feast: four cups of wine, the child's questions, the retelling that begins in disgrace and ends in praise by expounding Deuteronomy 26:5-8 (m. Pesachim 10:4), and Rabban Gamaliel's rule that one must speak of the Passover offering, the unleavened bread, and the bitter herbs (m. Pesachim 10:5). A roasted bone on the Seder plate recalls the lamb. The Samaritans, who hold Mount Gerizim to be the chosen place, still slaughter and roast Passover lambs there each year, the only community that keeps the sacrifice itself.
literary:
The chapter weaves narrative and instruction together. The events of the night take only eight verses (29-36), while instructions surround them: for the first Passover (1-13), for the Feast of Unleavened Bread in later years (14-20), for the elders (21-28), and for who may eat (43-49). The weaving is deliberate. The event is told so that it can be kept, and the phrase “for the generations to come” recurs (verses 14, 17, and 42). Verse 26 imagines a child asking, “What does this service mean to you?” It is one of four such questions in the Torah (12:26; 13:8, 14; Deuteronomy 6:20), and the Passover Haggadah, the order of service for the Jewish Passover meal, builds its teaching of four sons on them.

Two reports of obedience frame the night: “the Israelites went and did just what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron” (verse 28), and the same sentence almost word for word in verse 50. Israel obeys before anything has happened, in contrast to Pharaoh's ten refusals. Other details carry weight. The first commandment given to Israel as a people is about time (verse 2), and Rashi opens his whole Torah commentary by asking why Scripture did not begin here. The cry of the enslaved (3:7, 9) becomes a great cry in Egypt (verse 30), the same noun. Pharaoh, who asked “Who is the LORD?” (5:2), now tells Moses to go and serve the LORD and ends his last speech, “And bless me also” (verse 32), the reverse of the promise that Abraham's seed would be a blessing (Genesis 12:3). The verb avad, used for Israel's slave labor, becomes the word for its worship, “this service” (verses 25-26). Israel marches out as “the LORD's divisions” (verse 41), an army leaving at the end of the 430 years “to the very day”, and because the LORD “kept a vigil” that night, Israel keeps it as a vigil too (verse 42), the Hebrew shimmurim naming both God's watching and theirs.

Source critics usually assign the ordered instructions of verses 1-20 and 43-51 to the priestly source and the narrative of the elders and the night (21-39) to an older strand, and point to the repetitions as signs of combination. Commentators who read the final form, such as Brevard Childs (1974) and Terence Fretheim (Exodus, Interpretation, 1991), see the interleaving of liturgy and story as the point: Exodus presents the rescue in a form shaped for worship, so that later readers do not simply hear about the night but keep it.

outline.t: The first Passover: the lamb and the blood
The Feast of Unleavened Bread for all generations
Moses instructs the elders, and the people worship
The death of the firstborn and Israel's release
From Rameses to Succoth after 430 years

doctrines.note: Israel's firstborn are protected by the blood of a lamb that dies in their place, and the rite is called “the Passover sacrifice to the LORD” (verse 27). Israel's safety rests not on its own innocence but on the blood God provided, a pattern the sacrificial laws of Leviticus develop (Leviticus 17:11) and the New Testament sees fulfilled in Christ, “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Interpreters differ over whether the Passover is itself an atoning sacrifice or a protective covenant meal, and the text supports both emphases.

The Passover is a meal commanded as a memorial for all generations (verse 14), in which each generation takes part in the original rescue (13:8). Jesus instituted the Lord's Supper at a Passover meal and spoke of “the new covenant in My blood” (Luke 22:20). Christians differ over how Christ is present in the Supper, from a memorial of his death to a real sharing in his body and blood, but they agree that it proclaims his death as the fulfillment of what the Passover anticipated.

“I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt” (verse 12). The last plague falls not only on Egypt's people but on the powers Egypt trusted, including the divine king whose own heir dies (verse 29). It answers Pharaoh's order to drown Israel's sons (1:22) and fulfills a warning given long before (4:22-23). Judgment and rescue happen on the same night by the same hand.

Before Israel has a tabernacle, priesthood, or law code, God gives it a calendar (verse 2) and a rite. The word avodah, used for Israel's slavery, becomes the word for “this service” of worship (verses 25-26): Israel is freed from serving Pharaoh to serve the LORD. Worship begins with the ordering of time and of the household around what God has done.

The people who leave Egypt already include “a mixed multitude” (verse 38), and the Passover law opens Israel's central rite to any foreigner who takes the covenant sign: “he shall be like a native of the land”, and “The same law shall apply to both the native and the foreigner” (verses 48-49). Israel is defined by covenant membership, not by birth alone.

words.note: Pesach, Passover, about 49 occurrences in the Old Testament. It names the event (“it is the LORD's Passover”, verse 11, its first appearance), the festival, and the animal itself (“slaughter the Passover lamb”, verse 21). Through the Aramaic form it passed into Greek as pascha, the word the New Testament uses for the feast and the lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), and Greek-, Latin-, and Romance-speaking churches still call Easter by it. Melito of Sardis connected pascha with the Greek paschein, ‘to suffer’, a wordplay rather than an etymology, as Origen later recognized.

Pasach, the verb behind pesach, used in this sense only in verses 13, 23, and 27 and in Isaiah 31:5. Most translations take it as the LORD passing by or skipping the marked houses. Others point to Isaiah 31:5, where the LORD will protect Jerusalem “Like birds hovering overhead” and “will pass over it and preserve it”, and to the Septuagint's rendering in verse 13, skepasō, ‘I will shelter’, and argue for the sense stand guard over or protect. Both senses fit verse 23, where the LORD passes over the door and does not allow the destroyer to enter. A different verb of the same spelling means to limp (1 Kings 18:21).

Matstsah, unleavened bread, about 53 occurrences, flat bread baked without leaven. It was the bread of haste, since the people left before their dough could rise (verses 34 and 39), and the Feast of Unleavened Bread (chag hammatsot) takes its name from it. Because a small piece of leaven works through a whole batch, leaven became a picture of the way corruption spreads, and Paul urges the church to keep the feast “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth” (1 Corinthians 5:8).

Dam, blood, about 360 occurrences. It appears six times in verses 7-23. In the Old Testament blood stands for life given up in death: Leviticus 17:11 says the life of a creature is in the blood and that God has given it on the altar to make atonement. Here blood is ‘a sign for you’ (verse 13), marking the houses under God's promise, and Hebrews remembers Moses keeping “the Passover and the sprinkling of blood” by faith (Hebrews 11:28).

Zikkaron, a memorial or reminder, about 24 occurrences. The Passover day is to be “a memorial for you” (verse 14). In the Bible remembering is not merely recalling a fact but acting on it and taking part in it, so that each generation keeping the Passover says, “This is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt” (13:8). The Septuagint renders zikkaron with mnēmosynon, and the related Greek word anamnēsis is the one Jesus uses at the Last Supper, “do this in remembrance of Me” (Luke 22:19).

Tamim, whole, complete, unblemished, about 90 occurrences. For animals it means free of the defects listed in Leviticus 22:20-25, and it is required of nearly every sacrifice. For people it means integrity: Noah was tamim (Genesis 6:9), and God tells Abraham to be tamim (Genesis 17:1). The unblemished lamb of verse 5 stands behind Peter's description of believers redeemed “with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19).

Shachat, to ruin or destroy, about 150 occurrences. Verse 13 speaks of no plague ‘to destroy’ (lemashchit), and verse 23 turns the participle into a noun, hammashchit, ‘the destroyer’, whom the LORD will not allow to enter the marked houses. The same participle names the angel who struck Jerusalem in 2 Samuel 24:16. Interpreters differ over whether the destroyer is an angel of judgment under God's command or a personification of the plague; Jubilees 49:2 later called them the forces of Mastema, and Hebrews speaks of “the destroyer of the firstborn” (Hebrews 11:28).

Erev, a mixture, in the phrase erev rav, ‘a great mixed company’ (verse 38). A crowd of non-Israelites left Egypt with Israel. The text does not say who they were; they may have included other foreign laborers and Egyptians who had come to fear the LORD (9:20). Nehemiah 13:3 uses the word for people of foreign descent. Their presence explains why the Passover rules at once address foreigners (verses 43-49); later Jewish tradition, followed by Rashi, blamed them for the golden calf.

christ:
The New Testament reads Jesus' death through this chapter more than through any other in Exodus. John the Baptist introduces Jesus with the words “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), which gathers the Passover lamb together with the servant led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7) and the daily offerings. Paul writes, “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and draws the conclusion from verse 15: the house must now be cleared of leaven. Peter speaks of believers redeemed “with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19), echoing verse 5. Revelation's central figure is a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, praised because “by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation” (Revelation 5:6, 9), a people drawn from all nations as the Passover law already opened the meal to foreigners (verse 48).

John's account of the crucifixion is full of this chapter. He dates Jesus' death to “the day of Preparation for the Passover” (John 19:14), when the lambs were being killed; he notes that the sponge of sour wine was lifted to Jesus on hyssop (John 19:29), the plant that applied the blood; and he reports that the soldiers did not break Jesus' legs, seeing in it the fulfillment of Scripture: “Not one of His bones will be broken” (John 19:36), which draws on the rule of verse 46 (and Numbers 9:12) together with Psalm 34:20.

Jesus himself chose a Passover meal to institute the Lord's Supper. “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering”, he says, and then over the cup, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:15, 20). The Gospels describe the timing differently: Matthew, Mark, and Luke present the Last Supper as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12), while John places the crucifixion on the day the lambs were killed. Joachim Jeremias (The Eucharistic Words of Jesus) argued at length that the Supper was a Passover meal; others think John's dating is historical and the Synoptic meal was held a day early, or that different calendars were in use, or that John's timing is chiefly theological. All four Gospels tie Jesus' death to the Passover.

There is also a deeper and more costly pattern, thematic rather than predictive. The tenth plague fell because Pharaoh would not release God's firstborn son, Israel (4:22-23). In the New Testament God does not take the firstborn of his enemies but gives his own Son, “the firstborn over all creation” (Colossians 1:15), and the Passover's promise, that judgment passes over those who shelter under the blood God provides, is extended to all who belong to him. Hebrews says Moses kept “the Passover and the sprinkling of blood” by faith (Hebrews 11:28), and the Christian Easter, called pascha in Greek, remembers the night of the exodus as the pattern of the night of the resurrection.
interpretation:
The chapter shaped Jewish practice and thought from early on. Ezekiel the Tragedian, a Jewish poet of Alexandria probably in the second century BC, staged the exodus as a Greek tragedy (the Exagoge), and his surviving lines include God's instructions for the Passover. The Book of Jubilees (chapter 49, second century BC) retells the night, names the killers of the firstborn as the forces of Mastema, a prince of evil spirits, and insists that the Passover be eaten at the sanctuary. The Wisdom of Solomon (18:14-16) pictures God's all-powerful word leaping from heaven at midnight like a warrior to strike the firstborn, lines the Latin church later used as an entrance chant in the Christmas season. Philo (Special Laws 2.145-149) noted that at Passover each layman acted as priest and read the feast as the soul's crossing from the passions to wisdom. The Mishnah tractate Pesachim sets out the temple slaughter and the household meal; the Mekhilta's tractate Pisha comments on the chapter verse by verse; the Aramaic Targum Neofiti expands verse 42 into a poem of four nights, creation, the covenant with Abraham, the exodus, and the final redemption; and the Haggadah, whose early development from Mishnah Pesachim 10 Baruch Bokser traced in The Origins of the Seder (1984), stresses that God acted in person that night, not through an angel or messenger.

Christians made the chapter the lens for Easter. Melito of Sardis's homily On the Pascha (about 160-170) reads Exodus 12 line by line as a figure of Christ's death, though its harsh accusations against Israel have rightly troubled later readers. Melito belonged to the Quartodecimans of Asia, who kept Easter on the fourteenth of Nisan; around 190 Polycrates of Ephesus defended that custom against Victor of Rome, who wanted a Sunday observance, and the Council of Nicaea in 325 settled on a common Sunday reckoning. The Easter Vigil's Exsultet proclaims ‘this is the night’ when God led Israel out of Egypt, and speaks of the true Lamb whose blood consecrates the doorposts of believers. Thomas Aquinas's sequence for Corpus Christi, Lauda Sion (about 1264), names the paschal lamb among the figures of the Eucharist, and Martin Luther's Easter hymn Christ lag in Todesbanden (1524), set by Bach as Cantata 4, sings of the true Easter Lamb whose blood marks our door so that the destroyer cannot touch us.

Modern critical scholarship has asked about origins. Julius Wellhausen and, influentially, Leonhard Rost (1943) argued that the Passover began as a shepherds' spring rite, protecting households and flocks when they moved to new pasture, later joined to the exodus and to an agricultural Feast of Unleavened Bread; J. B. Segal (The Hebrew Passover, 1963) proposed instead an ancient New Year festival. Many scholars now doubt that Israel's nomadic past can be reconstructed with such confidence. Jewish and Christian commentators alike note that whatever its prehistory, Exodus gives the rite its meaning from the event.

In liturgy, Exodus 12:1-20 is read in the synagogue as Parashat HaChodesh before the month of Nisan, the whole chapter falls in Parashat Bo (Exodus 10:1-13:16), and 12:21-51 is the Torah reading on the first day of Passover. The Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 1-14 every year on Maundy Thursday. In art, Dieric Bouts painted the Passover meal as a side panel of his Altarpiece of the Holy Sacrament in Leuven (1464-1468), the family standing around a roasted lamb, staffs in hand; Handel's oratorio Israel in Egypt (1739) sets the death of the firstborn as a hammering chorus. The Talmud's reflection that God rebuked the angels for singing while Egyptians drowned (b. Megillah 10b; Sanhedrin 39b), and the Seder custom of removing drops of wine at the naming of the plagues, show how Jewish tradition has held rescue and the suffering of enemies together.
text:
Verse 40 has a real textual difference. The Masoretic Text, the standard Hebrew, says the Israelites lived in Egypt 430 years. The Septuagint reads ‘in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan’, and the Samaritan Pentateuch ‘in the land of Canaan and in the land of Egypt’, both counting from Abraham's arrival in Canaan. On that reckoning the stay in Egypt itself lasted about 215 years, the figure Josephus gives (Antiquities 2.318), and Paul's statement that the law came 430 years after the promise (Galatians 3:17) fits it, as do the short genealogy of Exodus 6:16-20 and the ‘fourth generation’ of Genesis 15:16. Those who keep the Masoretic figure point to the four hundred years of Genesis 15:13 and Acts 7:6 and take the genealogies as selective. Most text critics regard the Masoretic reading as original and the Greek and Samaritan readings as harmonizing.

In verse 22 the word saf can mean ‘basin’ or ‘threshold’. Most English versions read ‘basin’; the Septuagint and Vulgate read ‘threshold’, which would mean the animal was killed at the doorway and the whole frame was marked. In verse 13 the Septuagint renders the verb pasach as ‘I will shelter’ (skepasō), and Targum Onqelos with a verb meaning ‘I will spare’. Other differences are matters of translation. Verse 3 reads ‘lamb’ in most versions, though the Hebrew seh includes kids (verse 5). ‘Between the two evenings’ (verse 6) appears as ‘in the evening’ (KJV), ‘at twilight’ (ESV, BSB), or ‘at dusk’ (NRSV). Verse 38's ‘mixed multitude’ (KJV, ESV) becomes ‘many other people’ (NIV) or ‘a mixed crowd’ (NRSV). Verse 41's ‘hosts’ (KJV, ESV) is ‘divisions’ in the BSB and NIV. The verse numbering of the chapter is the same in Hebrew and English Bibles.

teach.big: God rescues his people from judgment and slavery through the blood of a substitute he provides, and he gives them a meal of remembrance so that every generation can know the rescue as its own.

outline.t: Redemption reorders time: Israel's year begins with what God does for them, not with the harvest or the king.
Deliverance comes through a whole, unblemished life given in the household's place, and through trusting God's word enough to mark the door and stay inside.
The rescue is to be relived, not only recalled, and the feast calls for clearing out the old leaven: remembrance reshapes how the redeemed live.
Faith is handed on in households through questions and answers, and obedience comes before the promise is fulfilled.
Judgment falls on those who refused God's warnings, the oppressor's grip is broken, and the enslaved leave paid rather than empty-handed.
God keeps his word to the very day, and the night he watched over Israel becomes a night Israel keeps watch for him.
The covenant meal belongs to those who belong to the covenant, and it is open on equal terms to every outsider who comes under its sign.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first allegorizes every detail, making the four days, the hyssop, the roasting, and the staff each stand for a separate Christian truth. The New Testament draws specific lines (the lamb, the blood, the unbroken bones, the leaven) and a teacher should follow those rather than invent more. The second flattens the Passover into a simple picture of the cross with no life of its own. The chapter is first a Jewish feast, still kept, and Christians honor the text best by learning how Israel has kept it rather than by treating it as a prop.

A third error uses the chapter to set Christians against Jews. Melito's homily and much medieval preaching turned the Passover into an accusation against the Jewish people, and that history should make Christian teachers careful: the New Testament's use of the Passover is a claim about Jesus, not a charge against Israel. A fourth skips the moral difficulty of verse 29 or treats it as a triumph to celebrate. Scripture itself, and Jewish tradition after it, holds rescue and grief together. Finally, avoid presenting the blood as a magic charm. Verse 13 says it is a sign ‘for you’, and Hebrews 11:28 places its power in faith in God's word, not in the substance on the door.
teach.pastoral: The death of the firstborn will be hard to hear for parents who have lost a child, and a teacher should not hurry past it or treat it as a victory lap. Name the cost honestly, set it within the long story of Pharaoh's own murder of Israel's sons and his repeated refusals, and let people grieve. For those who carry shame or a sense that they are not good enough to be spared, the chapter's point is freeing: Israel's houses were passed over not because the people inside were better than the Egyptians but because of the lamb's blood. The household questions of verses 26-27 may also press on parents whose children have walked away from faith; the text puts the child's question at the center and does not assume that every child will ask it the same way, as the Haggadah's four sons recognize.

hard.q: How could a just God kill the firstborn of Egypt, from Pharaoh's heir to the prisoner's son?
hard.a:
The objection is strong and should be stated fully. Verse 29 describes the death of every firstborn son in Egypt, including children and prisoners who had no part in Pharaoh's decisions, and even the animals. Richard Dawkins (The God Delusion, 2006) placed infanticide in his catalogue of the Old Testament God's crimes, and many readers who are not hostile to faith find the verse the hardest in the book. Within Judaism the difficulty was felt early: the Talmud tells that God silenced the angels who wished to sing as the Egyptians drowned, saying that the work of his hands was dying (b. Megillah 10b; Sanhedrin 39b), and the Seder custom of spilling wine at the naming of the plagues has often been explained as lessening joy at an enemy's suffering.

Several responses are given, usually together. First, the plague is presented as judgment answering a crime. Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile (1:22), and God warned him at the start that because he would not release God's firstborn son, Israel, his own firstborn would die (4:22-23); nine plagues and many chances to relent preceded it. Rabbinic interpreters often read the plagues as measure for measure. Second, the target is also Egypt's gods and divine kingship (verse 12): Pharaoh's heir was the next god-king, and the blow exposes the powers Egypt trusted. Third, Israel was not exempt by nature. Its firstborn were spared only under the blood and were afterward claimed by God and redeemed (13:1-2, 13), which suggests that the death of the firstborn is a judgment all deserve and from which all need rescue. Fourth, Scripture holds that God, who gives life, has the right to take it (Deuteronomy 32:39), and death came to Egypt's firstborn as it comes to every human being, though here as a sign. Terence Fretheim (Exodus, 1991) reads the plagues as creation itself turning against a regime that had violated God's order of life. Christian readers add that the God of Exodus finally gives his own Son rather than taking the sons of others.

None of these responses makes the verse easy, and some thoughtful Christians, while confessing God's justice, admit that it remains a place where they must trust what they cannot fully see. Skeptical readers who judge the account unhistorical still face the moral question of why Israel told the story this way, and Jewish tradition's own answer has been to remember the night with gratitude and with grief.

hard.q: What did the Passover blood mean, and where did the rite come from?
hard.a:
The historical-critical case is that the Passover is older than the exodus story. Julius Wellhausen connected it with the offering of firstlings, and Leonhard Rost (1943), comparing the customs of Arab pastoral nomads, argued that it began as a shepherds' rite at the spring move to new pasture: a family killed an animal at full moon, smeared blood on the tent entrance to ward off a demonic destroyer, and ate the meat roasted with unleavened bread before breaking camp. On this view Israel's tradition later joined the rite to the exodus and to the separate farmers' Feast of Unleavened Bread. Some scholars see the ‘destroyer’ of verse 23 as a trace of that earlier belief.

Responses come from several directions. Many scholars now judge Rost's reconstruction of early Israel's nomadic life too speculative, and J. B. Segal (1963) offered a quite different background, so the prehistory is uncertain. Those who read the chapter as describing the rite's institution see no need for a pagan background, and even those who accept one note that Exodus gives the rite an entirely new meaning: the blood protects because God has promised to see it (verse 13), not by magic, and the destroyer acts only under God's command (verse 23).

On the meaning of the blood itself, readers differ. Many Christian interpreters, and some Jewish ones, see substitution: Israel's firstborn were spared not because Israelites were better than Egyptians, but because a lamb had died in the house, the principle Leviticus 17:11 later states for all sacrificial blood. Others, including many Jewish commentators and some Christians, stress that the Passover is not a sin offering but a protective, covenant-marking meal whose focus is deliverance and belonging; the Mekhilta reads the blood of the Passover alongside the blood of circumcision as Israel's first acts of obedience. The text supports both emphases, since it calls the rite a sacrifice (verse 27) and centers it on a family meal, and Hebrews 11:28 locates its power in faith.

observe: What exactly are the Israelites told to do with the lamb, its blood, and the meal in verses 3-11, and how are they to be dressed when they eat?
What question does verse 26 expect children to ask, and what answer does verse 27 give?
Who is allowed to eat the Passover according to verses 43-49, and on what condition may a foreigner join?
interpret: Why do you think God began Israel's calendar with the month of the exodus (verse 2)? What does that say about how Israel was to understand its whole year?
Verse 13 says the blood would be ‘a sign for you’. What did the blood do, and what did it not do?
How does the New Testament use this chapter to explain Jesus' death, and which details does it draw on?
apply: The Passover was meant to be explained to children who ask what it means. How would you answer that question about the practices of your own faith?
Israel was protected not because they were better than the Egyptians but because of the lamb's blood. How should that shape the way you think of yourself and of people outside the faith?
The same law applied to the native-born and to the foreigner who joined Israel (verse 49). Who is treated as an outsider in your community, and what would it mean to welcome them as full members?
